17100:
A vestment is a special, ceremonial garment worn by a member of the clergy (such as a priest, bishop, deacon, or minister) during a religious service or sacred ritual. Think of it as a "religious uniform" — clothing that is put on specifically to perform religious duties, not worn as everyday clothing.

The word is most commonly used in the context of Christianity, but the concept of special garments worn during worship exists across many religions.

Not just any piece of clothing is a vestment. A true vestment has three defining qualities:

  1. It is ceremonial — worn only during a religious service, rite, or ritual, not during ordinary daily life.
  2. It signals a sacred role — by putting it on, the wearer is visually marking themselves as someone performing a holy function (leading a Mass, conducting a baptism, etc.).
  3. It carries symbolic meaning — the style, color, and design of a vestment are not random. They communicate something about the religious occasion, the rank of the wearer, or the time in the religious calendar.

To make this concrete, here are some well-known vestments you might encounter:

  • The Alb — A long, plain white robe reaching to the feet, worn as a base garment. The white color symbolizes purity.
  • The Chasuble — A large, sleeveless outer garment worn over the alb by a priest during the Eucharist (the central Christian ceremony). It is often richly decorated.
  • The Stole — A long, narrow strip of fabric worn around the neck and hanging down the front. It functions almost like a badge of office — deacons, priests, and bishops each wear it differently to signal their rank.
  • The Surplice — A loose, wide-sleeved white garment, often worn over a black cassock, common in Anglican and other Protestant churches.
  • The Mitre — The tall, pointed hat worn by a bishop. Yes, even a hat can be a vestment.
  • The Cassock — A long, fitted black (or sometimes white or red) robe worn by clergy, which can serve as an everyday clerical garment but also as a base for other vestments during services.

One of the most interesting things about vestments is that their color changes depending on the religious season or occasion. This is especially prominent in Catholic and Anglican traditions:

  • Purple/Violet — worn during Advent (before Christmas) and Lent (before Easter), seasons of reflection and penitence.
  • White or Gold — worn during Christmas, Easter, and other joyful celebrations.
  • Red — worn on Pentecost (celebrating the Holy Spirit) and on the feasts of martyrs (saints who died for their faith). Red symbolizes fire and blood.
  • Green — worn during "Ordinary Time," the regular weeks of the year that fall outside special seasons.
  • Black — sometimes worn at funerals.

This means that simply by looking at the color of the priest's vestment, a worshipper immediately knows something about what kind of day it is in the religious calendar.

You will very often see the word in its plural form — "vestments" — because clergy typically wear several garments layered on top of one another during a service. Each layer has its own name and purpose. So when someone says "the priest put on his vestments," they mean he dressed himself in the full set of ceremonial garments required for that particular service.

There is also a room in a church called the "vestry" — this is the dedicated room where vestments are stored and where clergy get dressed before a service.

While the word is most heavily associated with Christianity, the idea of a special sacred garment exists in most world religions:

  • Jewish high priests historically wore elaborate sacred garments (described in detail in the Bible).
  • Hindu priests wear specific garments during puja (worship).
  • Buddhist monks wear robes that are their sacred vestments.

However, the word "vestment" itself is almost exclusively used when talking about Christian clergy. For other religions, you would typically use terms like "ritual garments" or "sacred robes."

It helps to understand vestments by comparing them to similar concepts:

VestmentCostumeUniform
PurposeReligious/sacred dutyPerformance/entertainmentProfessional identification
ContextChurch/ritualStage/eventWorkplace
SymbolismDeep theological meaningCharacter or roleRank or team
  • A costume is worn to play a character or entertain. A vestment is not for entertainment — it is worn in sincere, sacred duty.
  • A uniform (like a police officer's) identifies your profession. A vestment goes further — it does not just say who you are, it says what holy act you are performing right now.
  • A vestment is unique because it transforms the act of getting dressed into something spiritually intentional. Many clergy traditions treat the act of putting on vestments as a form of prayer in itself.
How to Use the Word in a Sentence

• "The bishop entered the cathedral wearing his finest vestments, embroidered with gold thread."
  • "She noticed the priest's red vestment and knew it was Pentecost Sunday."
  • "The old vestments were stored carefully in the wooden chest in the vestry."
  • "Before the Mass began, the deacon helped the priest put on his vestments."

A vestment is a special ceremonial garment worn by clergy during religious services, chosen with great intentionality because its style, form, and color all carry deep symbolic and spiritual meaning — marking both the sacred role of the wearer and the nature of the religious occasion being celebrated.
17101: "Vet" is an informal, shortened word. It has two distinct meanings, and both are very common in everyday English. The context of a sentence almost always makes it clear which meaning is intended.

A vet is a doctor for animals. The full word is veterinarian, but almost everyone — in speech and in informal writing — shortens it to just "vet."

Just as a human doctor diagnoses illnesses, prescribes medicine, and performs surgery on people, a vet does all of those same things for animals. They study medicine for many years, earn a professional degree, and are licensed to treat animals.

What kinds of animals do vets treat?

Vets don't all treat the same types of animals. Most vets specialise in a particular group:

  • Small animal vets work mainly with pets — dogs, cats, rabbits, birds, guinea pigs, and so on. This is the kind of vet most people are familiar with. When your pet is sick or needs a vaccination, you take them to this type of vet.
  • Large animal vets (also called farm animal vets or livestock vets) travel to farms and treat cattle, horses, pigs, sheep, and other agricultural animals. They often visit the animals rather than having the animals come to a clinic.
  • Equine vets specialise specifically in horses.
  • Exotic animal vets treat unusual or wild animals — reptiles, zoo animals, wildlife, etc.

What does a vet actually do?

A vet performs a wide range of tasks:

  • Examining animals to figure out what is wrong with them
  • Diagnosing diseases and illnesses
  • Prescribing and administering medicine
  • Performing surgical operations
  • Giving vaccinations (commonly called "shots" or "jabs") to prevent disease
  • Setting broken bones
  • Advising pet owners and farmers on proper animal care, nutrition, and hygiene
  • Sometimes, when an animal is in severe and untreatable pain, performing euthanasia (humanely ending the animal's life) — this is also the vet's responsibility

Example sentences:

  • "My cat has been sneezing all week, so I booked an appointment at the vet."
  • "She always wanted to work with animals, so she trained to become a vet."
  • "The vet said the dog needs surgery on its leg."
  • "Our farm vet comes out every month to check on the herd."
Meaning 2: A Veteran (a former member of the military)

A vet also means a veteran — someone who has served in a country's armed forces (the army, navy, air force, marines, etc.), especially during a war or period of active conflict.

The word "veteran" itself simply means someone with long experience in a particular role, but when used on its own — and especially when shortened to "vet" — it almost always refers specifically to military service.

A vet in this sense is someone who has already completed their service and left the military (though the word can sometimes also describe currently serving soldiers informally). The focus is on the fact that they have been through military experience, particularly combat or wartime deployment.

In the United States, this meaning of "vet" is extremely common. Countries like the US, UK, Canada, and Australia have specific government departments, hospitals, benefits programmes, and support organisations dedicated to veterans — and in everyday talk, those people are simply called "vets."

Examples of how this is used:

  • "He's a Vietnam vet who served two tours of duty." (He is a veteran of the Vietnam War.)
  • "The government announced new healthcare benefits for vets."
  • "My grandfather is a vet — he served in the army during World War II."
  • "Many vets struggle to adjust to civilian life after returning from combat."
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Intended

Because both meanings are common, it's worth knowing how to tell them apart — though in practice it is almost always obvious from the surrounding words:

  • If the sentence is about animals, pets, a clinic, or animal health, "vet" means veterinarian.
  • If the sentence is about the military, war, a country's armed forces, or soldiers, "vet" means veteran.

You would never confuse:
"I took my dog to the vet" (clearly an animal doctor)
...with...
"He's a vet who served in Afghanistan" (clearly a military veteran).
A Small but Important Note: "Vet" Can Also Be a Verb

This is just a brief heads-up: "vet" is also used as a verb, where it means to carefully examine, investigate, or screen someone or something (e.g., "All candidates are thoroughly vetted before being hired"). That is a completely separate meaning and a different grammatical use — but it's good to be aware that the same word wears more than one hat in English.

In summary: As a noun, "vet" means either (1) an animal doctor (short for veterinarian), or (2) someone who has served in the military (short for veteran). Both meanings are informal but extremely widespread and considered perfectly standard in everyday English.
17102:
To vet something or someone means to carefully examine and investigate them — checking their background, history, claims, or suitability — before deciding whether to trust, approve, use, or accept them.

Think of it as a thorough, purposeful inspection done in advance, with a specific question in mind: "Is this person/thing reliable, safe, or good enough for what I need?"
What Makes "Vet" Different from Just "Check"

The word "check" is casual and broad. You check whether the lights are off. But "vet" carries a much stronger sense of scrutiny and judgment. When you vet something, you're digging deep, looking for problems, and ultimately making a serious decision based on what you find.

There's also a built-in purpose: you vet something because the stakes are high enough that a mistake would be costly. It's not a formality — it's a guard against risk.
Who Vets Whom, and What Gets Vetted

The verb works in a wide range of situations:

People vetting people:

  • A company vets job candidates before hiring them — checking their résumé, calling former employers, running a background check, and looking for anything concerning.
  • A government agency vets employees who will handle classified information — digging into their personal history, finances, relationships, and loyalty.
  • A person vets a contractor before letting them into their home — reading reviews, asking for references, checking licenses.

People vetting information or content:

  • A newspaper editor vets an article before publishing it — verifying facts, checking sources, and making sure nothing is misleading or legally risky.
  • A lawyer vets a contract before a client signs it — reading every clause carefully for hidden problems.
  • A researcher vets their sources before citing them — confirming the sources are credible, accurate, and not biased.

People vetting organizations or proposals:

  • A charity vets its donors to make sure it isn't accepting money from questionable sources.
  • An investor vets a startup before putting money in — examining its financials, team, and business model.
The Passive Form: "Vetted"

You'll often hear "vet" used in the passive voice — "he was vetted," "the information was vetted" — which simply means the vetting process has already happened and the person or thing has passed it (or, in some cases, been found wanting).

"All candidates are thoroughly vetted before being offered the position."
→ Every candidate goes through a rigorous examination process before the company makes a job offer.

"The intelligence report was never properly vetted."
→ Nobody took the time to carefully check whether the report was accurate or reliable.
The "Before" Element Is Everything

One of the most important things to understand about "vet" is its timing. Vetting always happens before a decision, a commitment, or an action. You vet someone before hiring them, not after. You vet a story before publishing it, not after. The whole point is to catch problems early, before they cause damage.

If the checking happens after something has already gone wrong, you wouldn't use the word "vet" — you'd say "investigate" or "audit" or "review."
The Question "Vet" Always Implies

Behind every use of this word is a specific, high-stakes question:

  • "Can we trust this person?"
  • "Is this information accurate?"
  • "Is this safe or suitable for our purpose?"
  • "Are there any hidden problems we should know about?"

Vetting is the process of answering those questions before it's too late.
How Thorough Is Vetting?

The depth of vetting depends on context. Vetting a plumber for a small repair job might just mean reading online reviews for ten minutes. Vetting a candidate for a senior government intelligence role might take months and involve interviews, polygraph tests, and extensive background investigations.

What stays constant is the seriousness of intent. No matter the scale, vetting means you're genuinely trying to find out the truth — not just going through the motions.
Common Patterns You'll Encounter

• "rigorously vetted" — the process was extremely thorough
  • "carefully vetted" — the process was done with close attention
  • "the vetting process" — the entire procedure of examining someone or something
  • "failed to vet" — someone skipped or poorly performed the examination, usually with bad consequences
  • "poorly vetted" — the examination was done carelessly or incompletely
A Few Sentences to See It in Action

1. "The producer did not vet the story properly, and the documentary turned out to contain several factual errors."
  2. "Before we partner with any new supplier, we vet them thoroughly — checking their financial stability, their safety record, and their reputation in the industry."
  3. "He was vetted for a top-secret security clearance and passed without any issues."
  4. "I always vet sources before using them in my writing. Just because something appears on a website doesn't mean it's true."
  5. "The campaign suffered after it emerged that the candidate's team had failed to vet her past statements."
The Underlying Attitude

There's a slightly cautious, even skeptical attitude built into the word. When you vet someone, you're not assuming they're trustworthy — you're finding out whether they are. It reflects the idea that trust should be earned and verified, not given automatically.
Summary in One Sentence
To vet something or someone is to carefully investigate and scrutinize them before making a decision — checking for problems, confirming reliability or suitability, and ensuring it's safe to proceed.
17103:
When "veteran" is used as an adjective, it describes a person who has spent a long time doing something and, as a result, has become deeply experienced, highly capable, and battle-tested in that area. The word tells you that this person has not just dabbled in something — they have lived it, faced its challenges repeatedly, and come out the other side shaped and sharpened by it.

Think of it this way: imagine two doctors. One graduated last year. The other has been treating patients for 25 years, has handled rare diseases, medical emergencies, and situations no textbook could have fully prepared them for. The second doctor is a veteran doctor. The word signals that their experience is deep, real, and earned — not theoretical.

"Veteran" as an adjective carries several powerful layers of meaning all at once.

Experience over a long period of time. It is not enough to have done something briefly. A veteran has put in years, sometimes decades. The passage of time is important because it means the person has seen many situations, not just one or two.

Real-world exposure, especially to difficulty. A veteran hasn't just practiced in safe or easy conditions. The word quietly suggests that the person has been tested — under pressure, in tough circumstances, in the real arena. This is why the word feels weightier than simply saying "experienced."

Skill and reliability that comes from that exposure. Because a veteran has been through so much, you naturally trust them. They don't panic easily. They've seen it before. They know what to do. A veteran journalist, for example, won't freeze up when a story gets complicated — they've covered difficult stories for years and know how to handle it.

A sense of respect. Calling someone a "veteran" is almost always a compliment. It is a word that society uses to honour someone's depth of experience. You are essentially saying: this person has earned their status. They didn't just show up — they put in the time and the work.

This is important to understand: although many people associate the word "veteran" with the military (since a "veteran" as a noun often means someone who served in the armed forces), the adjective form is far broader. It can be applied to virtually any field or activity.

A few examples to make this vivid:

  • "A veteran politician" — someone who has been in politics for many years, understands how power works, knows how to navigate complex situations, and has survived many elections and crises.
  • "A veteran actor" — someone who has been performing for decades, has taken on many roles, understands the craft deeply, and brings a calm, assured presence to their work.
  • "A veteran teacher" — someone who has spent many years in the classroom, has taught hundreds of students, handled all sorts of challenges, and knows instinctively what works and what doesn't.
  • "A veteran reporter" — a journalist who has spent years in the field covering all kinds of stories, often under difficult conditions, and has earned a reputation for knowing how to find and tell the truth.
  • "A veteran player" — in sports, an athlete who has played the game for many seasons, been through victories and defeats, understands the game at a deep level, and often serves as a steady, calming presence for younger teammates.

In every single case above, the word is doing the same job: it tells you that this person has been around, has seen a lot, and has grown because of it.

Getting clear on what a word does not mean is just as important as knowing what it does mean.

It does not simply mean "old." A person can be veteran at something at a relatively young age if they started early and have put in intense, consistent work over time. Age alone does not make someone a veteran — experience does.

It does not mean "retired" or "past their prime." A veteran can be fully active and at the height of their powers. The word says nothing about whether the person is still working — only about how deep their experience is.

It does not mean "the best." A veteran is respected for their experience, not necessarily ranked as number one. There could be someone newer who is technically more skilled. "Veteran" is about depth and time, not about being the greatest.

It is not the same as "expert." An expert is someone with a very high level of skill or knowledge. An expert could be young, self-taught, or lacking in real-world exposure. A veteran, on the other hand, always implies years of hands-on experience. All veterans tend to be experts in their area, but not all experts are veterans.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

"Veteran" is a warm, respectful, and dignified word. When you use it to describe someone, you are honouring them. It carries a quiet weight — the kind of weight that only comes from years of doing something real. It is the opposite of words like "novice," "rookie," "beginner," or "newcomer."

When you read or hear "veteran" before a person's title, your brain should immediately picture someone calm, capable, seasoned, and trustworthy — someone who has, in a sense, seen it all in their field and is no longer surprised or rattled by the ordinary challenges that come with it.
A Simple Way to Remember It

Whenever you see or hear the adjective "veteran," ask yourself: Has this person put in years of real, hard experience in this area? If yes, that's exactly what the word is pointing to. It is experience that has been lived deeply, tested by reality, and turned into quiet, unshakeable capability.
17104: A veteran is someone who has a lot of real experience in something — usually gained over a long period of time, and often in tough or demanding conditions. The word carries a strong sense of earned wisdom: this is not just someone who knows about something, but someone who has lived through it repeatedly and come out wiser for it.

The word "veteran" is used in two closely related but distinct contexts:

1. A Military Veteran

This is the most common and most specific use of the word.

A military veteran is a person who has served in a country's armed forces — the army, navy, air force, marines, etc. — and has completed that service (or is no longer actively serving). The word almost always implies they served during a real conflict or war, though it can apply to anyone with significant military service.

Think of it this way: a person who trained for six weeks and never left their home base would rarely be called a veteran. But someone who deployed to a warzone, endured hardship, and served their country under real pressure — that person is a veteran in the fullest sense of the word.

Examples: "The parade honored the veterans of World War II." / "She is a veteran of the Iraq War."

This use of the word is so dominant that in everyday speech, if someone simply says "a veteran" without any extra context, most people will automatically picture a military veteran.

2. A Veteran of Any Field or Profession

The word is also used more broadly to describe anyone with deep, long-standing experience in any area of life — not just the military. Here, the "battle" is metaphorical: it could be years of hard work, competition, challenges, or simply time spent doing something at a high level.

Examples: "She is a veteran of the film industry." / "He's a veteran teacher with 30 years in the classroom." / "As a veteran of many negotiations, she knew exactly what to do."

In this sense, calling someone a veteran is a mark of respect. It signals: "This person has been around. They've seen it all. They know what they're doing."
What Makes Someone a "Veteran" — The Key Ingredients

The word isn't thrown around lightly. For someone to truly deserve the title "veteran," there are a few invisible qualities that the word quietly implies:

  • Time — You have spent a significant amount of time in this role or field. A beginner is never a veteran.
  • Experience — Not just passive time, but active, real-world experience. You've faced real situations, real pressure, real challenges.
  • Hardship or difficulty — There's a subtle suggestion that it wasn't easy. Veterans have been through something.
  • Wisdom gained — Because of all of the above, a veteran knows things that a newcomer simply cannot know yet. Their experience has taught them lessons.

"Veteran" is almost always a positive, respectful word. When you call someone a veteran, you are nodding to their journey. You are saying, "This person has paid their dues. They have earned their place."

It is the opposite of words like rookie, novice, newcomer, or beginner — all of which describe someone at the start of their journey. A veteran is someone near the other end: seasoned, tested, and trusted.

At its simplestSomeone with a great deal of real, hard-earned experience
Most common useA person who has served in the military
Broader useAn experienced person in any field or walk of life
The feeling it carriesDeep respect for time served and lessons learned
One Sentence to Remember It By
A veteran is someone whose experience isn't just long — it's lived, tested, and earned.
17105:
A veterinarian is a trained medical doctor — but for animals, not humans. Just as a doctor examines, diagnoses, and treats sick or injured people, a veterinarian does the same for animals. They study medicine for years, earn a professional degree, and are legally qualified to provide medical care to animals.

The word is often shortened in everyday speech to "vet." Both words mean exactly the same thing.

A veterinarian's work covers everything that a human doctor's work covers — just applied to animals:

  • Diagnosis: A dog is limping, a cat is not eating, a horse has a fever. The vet examines the animal, runs tests, and figures out what is wrong.
  • Treatment: They prescribe medicines, perform surgeries, stitch wounds, set broken bones, and give injections.
  • Prevention: They give vaccines so animals don't get diseases in the first place. They advise owners on proper diet, hygiene, and habits.
  • Routine check-ups: They examine healthy animals regularly to make sure everything is fine — just like you visit a doctor for a general health check.
  • Emergency care: When an animal is in a sudden crisis — poisoned, hit by a vehicle, injured — the veterinarian handles the emergency.

This is an important part of the word's meaning. A veterinarian can, in principle, treat any animal — not just pets. The range includes:

  • Companion animals (the most common): dogs, cats, rabbits, hamsters, parrots, fish, turtles.
  • Farm and livestock animals: cows, goats, sheep, pigs, chickens. Here, a vet's work directly affects the food supply and the health of farming communities.
  • Horses: equine care is a large and specialized branch on its own.
  • Wild and zoo animals: lions, elephants, gorillas, dolphins — a zoo or wildlife sanctuary employs veterinarians to care for these animals.
  • Exotic pets: snakes, lizards, exotic birds, sugar gliders.

The word "veterinarian" covers all of these — the same title applies whether the person is treating your pet cat or performing surgery on a zoo elephant.

Just like in human medicine where you have cardiologists, dentists, and surgeons, veterinarians can specialize:

  • A veterinary surgeon performs complex operations.
  • A veterinary dentist deals with an animal's teeth and mouth.
  • A veterinary dermatologist treats skin conditions in animals.
  • An exotic animal vet focuses on unusual pets and wild species.
  • A large animal vet specializes in farm and agricultural animals.
  • A veterinary pathologist studies diseases — often to understand how illnesses spread, which sometimes helps protect human health too.

All of these people are still called "veterinarians." The specialization is an extra layer on top of the core identity.
An Important Distinction: Veterinarian vs. Similar Roles

The word "veterinarian" has a precise, protected meaning. Not everyone who works with animals is a veterinarian.

  • A veterinary nurse or vet technician assists the veterinarian — takes blood samples, monitors animals under anesthesia, prepares medicines — but is not qualified to diagnose or prescribe treatment independently.
  • A zookeeper feeds and cares for animals daily but is not a medical doctor.
  • A groomer cuts fur and cleans animals but has no medical role.
  • An animal trainer teaches behaviors but cannot treat illness.

A veterinarian, by contrast, is specifically someone with a medical degree in veterinary science and the legal authority to diagnose and treat animals.
The Broader Importance of the Role

Veterinarians are not just there for pet owners. They play a vital role in society:

  1. Public health: Many diseases jump from animals to humans (called zoonotic diseases — rabies, bird flu, etc.). Veterinarians monitor and control these diseases, directly protecting human populations.
  2. Food safety: They inspect meat, dairy, and eggs to ensure they are safe for people to eat.
  3. Scientific research: Veterinarians contribute to medical research, helping develop vaccines and treatments that sometimes benefit both animals and humans.
  4. Conservation: They work to protect endangered species and rehabilitate injured wild animals.
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

Seeing a word in real contexts helps fix its meaning firmly in your mind:

  • "My dog swallowed something dangerous, so I took him to the veterinarian immediately."
  • "She studied for eight years to become a veterinarian, specializing in large farm animals."
  • "The veterinarian examined the parrot and said it had a respiratory infection."
  • "Our local vet — a veterinarian with twenty years of experience — has treated hundreds of cats in this neighborhood."
  • "Veterinarians working at wildlife reserves must know how to handle animals that cannot be sedated easily."

Since you are a learner, it helps to know how this word connects to others in the same family:

  • Veterinarian (noun) — the person: "The veterinarian arrived quickly."
  • Veterinary (adjective) — relating to this field: "She is in veterinary school." / "This is a veterinary clinic."
  • Vet (noun, informal) — short for veterinarian: "I called the vet this morning." (Note: "vet" also informally means a military veteran, so context matters.)
  • Veterinary medicine (noun phrase) — the entire field or profession.

A veterinarian is a fully qualified animal doctor — someone with a medical degree who diagnoses, treats, and prevents illness and injury in animals of any species.

That single sentence, backed by everything above, is the complete picture of what this word means.
17106:
The adjective veterinary means relating to the medical care, health, and treatment of animals. Whenever you see this word, it is simply telling you: "this thing belongs to, or is connected with, the world of animal medicine."

Think of it this way: just as the word medical describes things related to human healthcare (a medical doctor, a medical clinic, medical advice), the word veterinary describes things related to animal healthcare. It is the animal-world equivalent of medical.

Veterinary applies to all animals — not just pets. This includes:

  • Companion animals like dogs, cats, and rabbits.
  • Farm and livestock animals like cows, pigs, sheep, and horses.
  • Wild animals like lions, eagles, or elephants (in zoos or wildlife rescue).
  • Exotic animals like reptiles, birds, and fish.

So it is not limited to your neighbor's pet dog. A zoo doctor treating a giraffe, a scientist studying disease in fish, and a nurse helping a cow give birth are all operating in the veterinary world.

As an adjective, veterinary is always placed in front of a noun to describe it. Here are the most common things it describes:

Veterinary medicine — the entire branch of science and practice dedicated to keeping animals healthy, diagnosing their illnesses, and treating them. It is the animal equivalent of human medicine.

Veterinary surgeon / veterinary doctor — the professional who is trained and qualified to treat animals. In everyday speech, people usually just call this person a vet. The full formal title is veterinary surgeon.

Veterinary clinic / veterinary hospital — the physical place where animals go to be examined and treated. Just like humans go to a hospital or clinic, sick or injured animals go to a veterinary clinic.

Veterinary care — the overall attention, treatment, and services provided to keep an animal healthy. "The injured bird received excellent veterinary care."

Veterinary science — the academic and scientific study of animal health, diseases, anatomy, and medicine.

Veterinary nurse / veterinary technician — a trained support professional who assists the veterinary surgeon, much like a nurse assists a human doctor.

Veterinary treatment — the specific procedures, medicines, or therapies given to an animal for a health problem.

Veterinary advice — guidance or recommendations given by a qualified animal-health professional about an animal's health.

Veterinary examination — a physical check-up of an animal done by a vet.

Veterinary practice — this can mean two things: (1) the act of practicing veterinary medicine as a profession, or (2) the business/office where a vet works.

• "She decided to study veterinary medicine because she loves animals."
  • "The dog was taken to a veterinary clinic after swallowing something dangerous."
  • "The farmer called for veterinary assistance when his horses fell ill."
  • "Veterinary science has advanced so much that animals can now have surgery similar to what humans receive."
  • "Always seek veterinary advice before giving your pet any medicine."
The Key Idea to Always Remember

If you ever see the word veterinary and feel unsure, just replace it in your mind with the phrase "to do with animal medicine" — and the sentence will make complete sense. It is always pointing you toward the world of animal health. That is its one, clear, consistent job as an adjective.
17107:
A veto is an official power or act of saying "No — this will not happen" in a way that is strong enough to stop or block a decision, even if everyone else agrees to it.

The key thing to understand right away is that a veto is not just a regular "no." When you or I say no to something, it can be overruled or ignored. But a veto is a special, authorised "no" — one that carries enough legal or official weight to actually stop something from going forward.

Think of it like a giant red STOP button that only certain people are allowed to press — and when they press it, the machine stops, no matter what.

Imagine a group of five friends voting on where to eat dinner. Four of them vote for pizza. But the fifth friend has a special rule that says his "no" can cancel the whole decision. So even though four people wanted pizza, that one person's "no" shuts it down entirely. That power — that official, decision-killing "no" — is a veto.

In more serious, real-world terms: a veto is the right or the act of blocking something that has been proposed or even already agreed upon by others.
The Two Faces of the Word

As a noun, "veto" can refer to two slightly different things, and it's important to know both.

First, it refers to the power or right itself — the authority someone holds to block decisions. For example: "The president has a veto over new laws." Here, "veto" means the official power that exists, whether or not it's been used yet.

Second, it refers to the act of using that power — the actual blocking of a specific decision. For example: "The president issued a veto." Here, "veto" means the concrete action of rejecting something.

So the word can describe the weapon itself, or the act of firing that weapon. Both uses are completely standard and correct.

In Government (The Most Famous Use)

The most well-known use of the veto is in politics. In many countries, a president or a monarch is given the power to reject a law that has been passed by the parliament or legislature. The lawmakers vote, they agree, they pass the bill — but then the head of state can say "no" and block it from becoming law. That act of rejection is called a veto.

In the United States, for instance, after the Congress passes a bill, the President can veto it, sending it back without signing it into law.

Now, here's an important nuance: a veto doesn't always mean "never." In many systems, a veto can be overridden — meaning if enough people in the group push back strongly enough (for example, a two-thirds majority), they can force the decision through anyway, overruling the veto. So a veto is powerful, but it is not always the final word. Whether it can be overridden or not depends entirely on the rules of the system in question.

At the United Nations

One of the most powerful vetoes in the world belongs to the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council — the United States, Russia, China, the United Kingdom, and France. If any one of these five countries casts a veto, a resolution (an official international decision) is blocked entirely, even if all the other member countries supported it. This veto cannot be overridden. It is absolute. This makes it a far stronger form of veto than most.

In Companies and Organisations

Vetoes also exist in the business world. A major shareholder, a board member, or a founding partner might be given veto power over certain company decisions. This means that even if the rest of the board agrees on something, that one person can stop it from happening.

In Everyday Life

The word "veto" is also used informally in everyday situations, outside of politics or law. A parent might say, "I have veto power over where we go on holiday," meaning they have the final say to reject any option they don't like. In this casual usage, the word keeps its core meaning — a powerful, decision-stopping "no" — but it's used loosely, without any official or legal weight behind it.
The Essential Qualities of a Veto

To truly understand what makes something a veto (and not just a regular objection), keep these three qualities in mind.

It must be authorised — the person using it must have been given the right to do so by a system, a set of rules, or a law. A random person cannot simply declare a veto.

It must be powerful enough to stop something — a veto has practical consequences. It doesn't just express disagreement; it actually blocks or cancels the decision.

It is typically used by one person or a small group — the whole point of a veto is that one voice can override many. If everyone had veto power equally, it wouldn't be special.
A Few Common Phrases You'll Encounter

"Veto power" — this refers to the right or authority to veto. Someone who has veto power can choose to use it or not use it. Simply having the power doesn't mean it has been used yet.

"To exercise a veto" — this means to actually use the veto, to carry out the act of blocking something. It's a slightly formal way of saying "to veto something."

"The veto was overridden" — this means the veto was challenged and defeated. The decision that was blocked went through anyway because enough people pushed back against the veto.

"A pocket veto" — this is a specific political term used in the United States. Normally, if a president does nothing with a bill — neither signs it nor vetoes it — it can become law on its own after a set number of days. But if Congress is not in session during those days, the president's inaction effectively kills the bill. This silent, do-nothing blocking is called a pocket veto, because the president essentially "pockets" the bill and does nothing. It's a veto achieved through silence rather than an active rejection.

The word veto captures a simple but profound idea: that in many systems — governments, organisations, families — not all voices carry equal weight when it comes to blocking decisions. A veto is the formalised, authorised power to say "This stops here," and to actually make it stop.

It is a tool of control, of balance, and sometimes of protection — used to prevent decisions that one party finds unacceptable, even when they are outnumbered. Whether it's a world leader rejecting a law, a nation blocking an international resolution, or a parent saying no to a holiday destination, the spirit of the word is always the same: one empowered "no" that can stop the many.
17108:
When you veto something, you officially and authoritatively reject or block a decision, plan, or law — stopping it from happening — even if other people have already agreed to it or voted for it.

The single most important thing to understand is this: a veto is not just a "no" from anyone. It is a powerful, formal "no" that actually kills or stops something. And only certain people, in certain roles, have the power to use it.

Imagine a group of people vote on a decision. The majority agrees. Everything seems settled. But then one specific person — someone with special authority — steps in and says, "I reject this. It will not go forward." That act of blocking it? That is a veto.

So to veto something is to:

  • Refuse to approve it, and
  • Use your authority to prevent it from taking effect.

Both parts matter. A regular person can refuse to approve something, but their refusal doesn't necessarily stop it. When someone vetoes it, their refusal does stop it — because they hold the power to do so.

In government (the most common context):

In many countries, a president or a monarch can veto a bill (a proposed law) that has been passed by the legislature (the parliament or congress). This means even though the lawmakers voted "yes," the president can step in and say "no," and the bill does not become a law.

For example: "The president vetoed the bill, so it never became a law."

In international bodies:

In the United Nations Security Council, five powerful countries (the US, UK, France, Russia, and China) each have the right to veto any major resolution. If even one of them vetoes it, the resolution is blocked — no matter how many other countries supported it.

For example: "Russia vetoed the resolution, so the Security Council could not take action."

In everyday informal use:

People also use "veto" more loosely in everyday life to mean firmly shooting down someone's idea — often humorously.

For example: "I suggested we go camping, but my wife vetoed it immediately."
Or: "The kids wanted pizza every night, but Dad vetoed that plan."

Here, the word still carries the same flavour — one person using their authority (as a spouse, a parent, a boss) to block what others wanted.
What a Veto Does NOT Mean

This is subtle but important:

  • Vetoing something does not always mean it is gone forever. In many systems, a veto can be overridden — meaning if enough people push back strongly enough (for example, a two-thirds majority in the US Congress), they can reverse the veto and make the decision stand anyway.
  • Vetoing something is not the same as simply disagreeing. You can disagree with something all you want, but you can only veto it if you have been given the formal authority to do so.
  • A veto is not a punishment. It is a mechanism — a built-in check — that gives certain people the power to block decisions they find unacceptable.

"Veto" carries a sense of finality and authority. When someone vetoes something, it lands with weight. It is decisive. It shuts a door. This is why the word is also used dramatically in casual conversation — when you veto your friend's bad idea for a road trip, you're borrowing that sense of firm, no-nonsense authority.
To veto something is to officially use your authority to reject and block it, preventing it from moving forward — regardless of who else agreed to it.
17109:
To vex someone means to cause them to feel annoyed, frustrated, or troubled — but with a very specific flavour worth understanding carefully.

It is not the sharp, explosive feeling of sudden rage. It is more of a persistent, nagging irritation — the kind that settles in and lingers. Think of vex as a slow simmer rather than a sudden boil.

Here's a simple picture: if someone bumps into you once by accident, you might feel a flash of irritation. That's not vex. But if the same person keeps interrupting you every time you speak, ignores your feelings, and repeats the behaviour again and again — that deep, building frustration you carry? That is what it means to be vexed.

Three things can vex a person:

A person can vex someone else. "His constant complaining vexed everyone at the table."

A situation can vex someone. "The hours-long traffic jam vexed the commuters greatly."

A problem or puzzle can vex someone. "The unsolved mystery vexed the detective for years." In this sense, vex means to baffle or perplex — to trouble the mind because something cannot be figured out. This use is slightly older and more formal, but you will encounter it in literature and careful writing.

Vex sits at a moderate level on the emotional scale. It is stronger than "slightly bother" but not as severe as "enrage." A rough scale to picture it:

mildly bother → irritate → vex → distress → infuriate

So if someone is vexed, they are genuinely bothered — not just mildly inconvenienced, but also not in a state of rage. They are somewhere in that uncomfortable middle ground of nagging frustration.

"The noise from the neighbours vexed him every morning." (A situation vexing a person)

"Her careless attitude vexed her supervisor." (A person's behaviour vexing another)

"The riddle had vexed scholars for centuries." (A problem baffling/troubling people)

"I was vexed to learn that my advice had been ignored." (Feeling annoyed about something)

Notice that vex is often paired with the person being affected as the subject when using the passive form: "I was vexed" rather than "something vexed me" — though both are correct.
Related Word Forms You Must Know

Vexed (adjective): This describes the state of feeling annoyed or troubled. "She wore a vexed expression." "He was vexed by the delay."

Vexing (adjective): This describes the thing or situation that is causing the annoyance. "It was a truly vexing problem." "His behaviour was vexing to everyone around him."

Vexation (noun): The feeling itself — the state of being vexed. "She struggled to hide her vexation." "It was a source of great vexation to him."

This is important. When someone calls something "a vexed question" or "a vexed issue," it does not mean the question is annoyed. It means the question or topic is one that has troubled people's minds for a very long time — it is deeply controversial, debated, and unresolved.

"The question of how to achieve lasting peace in the region remains a deeply vexed one."

This usage flows naturally from the original meaning: the issue has "troubled" so many minds, for so long, that it has become a vexed matter. You will see this phrase often in journalism, academic writing, and formal speech.

"Vex" has a slightly formal or literary flavour in standard English. In everyday casual conversation, people tend to say "annoyed," "frustrated," or "bothered" instead. You are more likely to read vex in a novel, an essay, or careful writing than to hear it in casual speech.

However, there is an important exception: in Caribbean English — spoken in Jamaica, Trinidad, Barbados, and other islands — "vex" is a completely everyday, informal word. There, it simply and directly means angry or upset. "She vex with me bad" means "she is very angry with me." This is a rich, living use of the word that you may encounter in Caribbean literature, music, and conversation.

To vex is to cause someone a persistent, nagging sense of annoyance, frustration, or distress — not a sudden explosion of anger, but a deep, simmering irritation that troubles them and stays with them.
